title: Google Research's Cogentic reports new proofs for five open math problems via multi-agent orchestration
subtitle: A new paper describes an iterative prove–verify loop that allocates independent prover agents across proof directions and uses adversarial verifiers to check their work.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google Research and Google DeepMind authors — Yang Cai, Vineet Gupta, Yanchen Jiang, Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Grigoris Velegkas and Di Wang — described Cogentic, a multi-agent harness for automated proof discovery on open research problems. An orchestrator allocates a population of independent provers across distinct proof directions; adversarial verifiers scrutinize each step; proven partial results are saved for later rounds. The paper reports new results on five open problems spanning online learning, auction theory and mechanism design, with each proof independently verified by a domain expert.

Cogentic uses Gemini 3.1 Pro and 4 Argon at roughly O(100) to O(1000) model calls per problem — small by the standards of today's search-heavy agents. The authors list concrete examples, including a regret bound for online inverse linear optimization. What is not in the paper is a Lean-style machine check: human experts confirmed the proofs, but no proof assistant mechanically re-verified them. The team flags that direction as future work.

The release fits inside a year in which agentic math has been the most-watched stress test for frontier models. AlphaProof Nexus, Aletheia and OpenAI's internal Erdős claim have all argued, in different languages, that chains of specialized agents can beat a single model at research-grade proof work. Cogentic's contribution is pragmatic — an orchestrator that spends more compute on parallelism and verification than on a single deep rollout, and that the authors can point to a project site to attest the results.

A note for learners: 'verified by a domain expert' is not the same as 'verified in Lean.' A human reviewer can miss a subtle gap; a proof assistant cannot. If you follow this field, read two things when a new agent proof lands — the problem statement, so you know what counts, and the verification method, so you know how far to trust the claim.
